DaviddTech’s ChatGPT bot search: the full method test

Correction (29 Sep 2026) · Protocol & corrections · Both clocks · All configurations · Reopen tests · Code & sources
CORRECTION — 29 September 2026

Some numbers on this page were wrong, and the mistake was ours. Our file of one-minute SPY prices held a few garbled prints: for example a one-minute high of 1,120.20 on 27 May 2005 and one of 9,195.00 on 20 May 2009, when SPY traded near 120 and 91. Our hourly search read those prices. The first bad print inflated the volatility measure our stop is built from, so the winning coin flip opened a trade on 27 May 2005 with its stop below zero (-3.16). That trade stayed open for almost four years and was scored as a win when it reached the 9,195.00 print. A second trade, opened a week after that print, was distorted the same way. The two trades were open for 20,644 of the 42,540 hours the search could see (48.5%).

How we found it: a later test moved the same winner into a second backtesting program, and that program refused to accept a stop price below zero.

What we did: We chose this repair rule after the original results were known. It is a post hoc correction, not part of the original daily pre-registration. We applied it before each re-run. We repaired the bad prints with one fixed rule (in the protocol table below), re-ran the unchanged search code, and checked that the same code on the unrepaired prices still gives the published numbers exactly. On the hourly clock the best coin flip is now a different version. It made +510.77% in the years the search could see and +36.05% in the years it could not, while simply holding SPY made +262.1%. So it did not lose money on the unseen years, as we first said (-11.50%). It made money and still trailed simply holding by 226.1 points. The configuration shown in the video (seed 95) still makes -11.50% on the unseen years after the repair; it simply is no longer the search's winner (it makes +123.56% on the seen years; these are our re-run results for the video's original configuration). The daily clock had 4 smaller bad prints of its own; repairing them barely moves it (its winner goes from +195.80% to +195.77% in the seen years, and is unchanged at +90.14% in the unseen years).

What still holds: a search across 2,048 coin-flip versions still produced a winner that looked like a discovery in the years it could see, and that winner still lost to simply holding the market, by a wide margin, in the years it could not. What does not hold: the hourly winner losing money, its -63.26% drawdown (now -51.36%), and our line that three of four predictions passed on the hourly clock. With a profit factor of 1.42, prediction 1 now misses its “above 1.5” clause, so it is two of four. Below, every corrected number shows the old one struck through. The video’s spoken and on-screen figures are the uncorrected ones; this page and the pinned comment carry the corrections.

Episode I05c · report format v2 · lab run 2026-07-14 · daily protocol and later hourly extension · corrected 2026-09-29
VERDICT — A searched winner is not yet evidence of predictive skill

Our hourly coin-flip winner went from +464.78% +510.77% in the search years to -11.50% +36.05% in unseen years. The daily companion went from +195.80% +195.77% to +90.14%, still 95.2 points behind holding. These are our SPY method demonstrations, with no costs in either side of either pair. They are not a test of his gold bot.

What we granted, and what we actually tested

Granted, not measured: His recommendations to use enough trades, evaluate unseen data and account for execution costs are sensible. A backtest can correctly compute what happened to the selected rules. We grant his screen as his reported output; we did not independently reproduce it. A properly designed forward test can add evidence.

Tested: Search 2,048 long-only, ATR-stop configurations on a signal independent of price; keep the highest historical return; carry that configuration into unseen years. We ran this procedure on SPY daily bars and a later hourly extension, not on gold and not through ChatGPT or his tools.

What this report does NOT claim: We did not run his strategy, validate his reported percentages, audit live trades, test the AI, database or chart platform, or prove that no searched strategy can work. His actual search width is unknown. Our demonstration does not establish anyone’s intent.

§1 · The daily protocol and its chronology

The daily protocol is dated 2026-07-14. The episode records a local timestamp six minutes before the first result; that is our timestamp and our word, not an independently sealed ordering. The protocol and both result files first entered our private repository together, in one commit. We do not publish its id because a reader could not open it; the ordering is therefore our word. There is no earlier separate lock in this history. The daily design is the pre-registration record; the hourly cut is a later extension, not pre-registered. The table below distinguishes what the protocol actually specified from run-stage choices.

The falsifiable question

Can a search across signals with no price information generate an impressive historical winner whose advantage over holding fails on unseen years?

  • A yes looks like: The selected historical winner stands above its search distribution and loses its benchmark margin in the unseen window.
  • A no looks like: A winner retaining its margin would trigger the original investigation rule; it would not by itself prove predictive skill or a simulator bug.
  • Ambiguous residue: A null signal can win by chance. These two windows are demonstrations, not a calibrated false-discovery probability or a statistical test of his bot.

Our stated prior: Search selection can create a convincing backtest from noise

That was the thesis in the daily protocol. Its strongest language overreached: the current claim is about how much evidence a selected backtest supplies, not a determination of the cause of his reported result.

Protocol and run-stage choices

ParameterValue and timing
Daily instrument and datesSPY, 2004-01-02 to 2024-12-31; protocol
Daily splitSearch through 2014-12-31; unseen 2015–2024; protocol
Entry signalSeeded Bernoulli probability, independent of price; next-bar-open execution; signal in protocol, execution in code
Search grid128 seeds × probabilities [0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.1] × ATR multiples [1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5] = 2,048; protocol
Risk and exitsLong only, one position; ATR(14); 3.8:1 target; 2% fixed-fractional risk; protocol. The 2% sizing is our convention, not a verified rule of his bot.
SelectionHighest in-sample compounded return; single winner; protocol
BenchmarkBuy-and-hold SPY in the same window; protocol. Close-to-close price return, excluding dividends; exact endpoint formula in code.
Random-number sequenceSeed base 20260714; base + seed × 131 + int(probability × 1000); exact offset formula is run-stage code
Friction0.05 R per completed round trip; costs promised in protocol, exact level chosen in code. Applied to in-sample trades only, not an OOS net-of-cost comparison.
OOS cross-sectionTop 50 by IS return plus every eighth IS rank (256 configurations); sample sizes and rank-based sampling chosen in code. 299 distinct OOS configurations per clock, because 7 overlap.
Hourly extension2003-09-10 12:00:00 to 2026-06-22 17:00:00 UTC; cut 2015-01-01; one-minute bars resampled to hours, all available sessions. Run-stage extension; not the registered daily dates.
Price repair (added 2026-09-29)We chose this repair rule after the original results were known. It is a post hoc correction, not part of the original daily pre-registration. We applied it before each re-run. Rows are never dropped. Minute rows are repaired in input file order before sorting and hourly aggregation; daily rows are repaired in date order after selecting the requested dates and ticker. (1) Compute close flags together from the original neighbouring closes, excluding the first and last rows: if the absolute value of close / neighbour - 1 exceeds 0.10 for both neighbours, replace both its close and its open with the original previous close. (2) Using the repaired closes, flag opens whose absolute ratio difference from both the previous close and their own close exceeds 0.10, excluding the first row; replace each flagged open with the repaired previous close. (3) Using the resulting open and close, replace a high above 1.10 times their maximum with that maximum, and a low below 0.90 times their minimum with that minimum. (4) Enforce final bounds: high is at least max(open, close), and low is at most min(open, close). See the public reproduction script for the exact implementation. It changed 13 of 4,185,928 one-minute rows and 4 of 5,285 daily rows.
Fill and terminal conventionsGaps at open; stop before target if both hit; no open-position mark-to-market at the window end. Numerical equity compounds completed trade returns. Implementation conventions; not a broker simulation.

Untested scope and when it was identified

  1. Gold at his resolution/session, his exact strategy, his database and AI tool: outside the daily design and still untested.
  2. Live results, the announced forward test and any causal conclusion about his process: not measured.
  3. Execution-cost calibration, terminal position valuation and larger independent replications: limitations identified from the implemented model, not retroactively called pre-registered.
The protocol required the distribution, unseen winner and friction results regardless of outcome. We preserve its original predictions and disclose the scoring error.

There was no numerical tolerance predeclared for “spectacular”, “about zero” or “same order of magnitude”. The score is therefore descriptive, not a preregistered significance test.

The original text remains evidence of what we wrote, including errors we now correct. Its references to a particular search width for him, an exact risk skeleton, a survivorship control, and a single lucky result necessarily being a bug are not assertions of this report. His career backtest count did not establish this search’s width; our sizing and execution conventions are ours. The source’s forward-test language was also too categorical: valid unseen evidence can change our assessment. Read the corrections above with the archive.

Read the four original predictions, verbatim
1. **Best-of-2,048 IS net% is spectacular** — same order of magnitude as his 1,669% (at minimum
   >> the median config), with WR ~20–35% and PF > 1.5: a config that *looks* like a real edge,
   and a large positive **IS alpha over B&H**.
2. **The winner's OUT-OF-SAMPLE alpha over B&H collapses to ~0 or negative** — because random
   entries carry no signal into unseen data. **THE KILL.** (Raw OOS return may stay positive from
   beta; the *alpha* is what must vanish.)
3. **IS rank does not predict OOS** — across the top-N IS configs, rank-correlation(IS net, OOS
   net) ≈ 0; and the share of all configs that beat B&H OOS is ~coin-flip.
4. **Friction bites** — with a realistic per-trade cost the median config's alpha is negative and
   the winner shrinks.

§4 · The controls

Signal generation is independent of price by construction. SPY’s upward price drift is why holding is the comparison. Calling a single ETF a survivorship-free control adds no evidence. The benchmark is unlevered price return; strategy sizing, time in market and risk differ, so the percentage-point margin is not risk-adjusted alpha.

ClockSample beating holding OOSSample sizeRate
Daily1 22560.4% 0.8%
Hourly extension19 202567.4% 7.8%

The 256 are a systematic sample of in-sample ranks, not a random sample, and not all 2,048 configurations. The top 50 are also selected on IS performance. Their near-zero rank relationships do not warrant a directional inference. No independence or confidence interval is claimed for these cross-sections.

§5 · The strongest objection and the implementation limits

The strongest objection is the instrument mismatch: SPY is not gold, its sessions are not the Asia filter, and its upward drift helps random long exposure. The hourly data comprise available US sessions, roughly 04:00–20:00 Eastern when present; empty hours are dropped. This does not reproduce a continuous 24-hour market. We also used different dates across clocks.

The engine compounds closed trades only; an open position at a window boundary is discarded rather than marked to market. The unseen segment starts flat. Stop/target ordering is a convention when both touch, and drawdown is measured on completed-trade equity, not every market move. Dividends, cash interest, taxes, latency, slippage calibration and financing constraints are absent. ATR uses preceding bars; signal execution is next-bar open. These limitations restrict the numerical comparison; they are not repaired by a random signal.

Selection among many correlated configurations is the demonstrated mechanism. We did not establish how many candidates his tool searched or the quality of those candidates. A transparent, frozen future evaluation could distinguish a useful strategy from this demonstration.

§6 · Their own terms

I Did It! I Found The BEST AI Trading Bot Ever (INSANE Results), Trading with DaviddTech, is the source tutorial. We ran the search method it demonstrates on a coin-flip signal; we did not run the strategy it found. The tutorial presents a database search, a backtest, a chart-platform parity check and a planned forward evaluation. Those are his reported objects, not our replications.

His checklist addresses enough trades, unseen evaluation and execution. We agree with those questions. Reproducing the same rules on another chart engine checks arithmetic; it does not create new observations. Fresh data must follow selection to test the selected winner fairly. Nothing here grades his personal record.

§8 · What would change our mind

  1. Committed bot’s full trade list: a bot chosen before its evaluation window, with hundreds of trades over a sufficiently long window, beating holding gold after costs. We would run that test and report the result. This is a future review criterion, not a test completed here.
  2. Frozen winner, future window: commit one selected configuration before fresh data exists, then compare it with holding after matched costs. Sustained positive excess return would challenge this demonstration’s conclusion. No such walk-forward was run here.
  3. The whole strategy database: publish the complete search population and selection history, including discarded strategies, so its selected winners can be evaluated against the search that produced them. We did not acquire or test that database.
  4. A reproducible error or repeated null excess return: the original protocol said to investigate a positive-OOS-alpha winner as a bug. That was too categorical: one null ticket can get lucky. The hourly sample’s success rate is not a calibrated probability for a new search winner. Repeated independent replications with a predeclared test would be evidence to investigate and could retract the finding.
  5. A larger, registered search or different market: a wider grid, true gold-session data or different windows could change the magnitude. These are unrun extensions, not claims that the current experiment matches his screen.

§9 · What survives

Keep the checklist. Ask whether the winner was selected before or after it saw the evaluation window. A useful strategy can survive that test; a spectacular selected backtest alone does not answer it.

The first three reopening criteria restate the episode’s offer; the error/replication and wider-search items are post-run review criteria. They are not retrospectively added to the daily protocol.

§10 · Tools for your own testing

Everything we make is free — the reports, the ledgers, all of it. The only thing that costs us real money is the market data.

Every numerical market input here is SPY equity-price history from Massive.com (formerly Polygon.io): daily OHLC for the daily cut and one-minute OHLCV resampled to hours for the extension. The buy-and-hold benchmark is computed from the same SPY closes. It excludes dividends. No separate benchmark vendor, cash-yield series, options data or gold data produced a number in this experiment. The specimen’s displayed figures are his report, not a market-data input to our results. EODHD, the affiliate below, supplied none of this test’s data; neither vendor has a say in the verdict.

Download the seeded reproduction code It preserves the original numerical functions and both experiment mains with portable file-input/output adapters. Supply your own licensed prices; raw vendor prices are not redistributed. Requires Python, NumPy, pandas and pyarrow. The command and schemas are in the file. The code regenerates both archived summary files field for field on the source data: 101 of 101 fields. 18 of those are copied inputs rather than results: the 8 search parameters, and the 10 figures from his screen, which the code copies and does not measure. The ticker, the hourly timeframe and cut labels, and the daily start, end and split dates are also set in the code rather than measured. Runtime depends on the computer and data. It writes the two original summary files; all configuration rows are supplied in the ledger above. Correction 2026-09-29: the code now applies the price repair in the protocol table by default and regenerates the corrected figures (101 of 101 fields); run with --raw it skips the repair and regenerates the figures as first published, bad prints included (101 of 101 fields).
